short: In 301 CE Diocletian fixed maximum prices for around 1,400 goods and wages across the empire, on pain of death, to check runaway inflation.
full:
In 301, Diocletian issued the Edict on Maximum Prices, setting ceilings for the cost of roughly 1,400 goods and services, from grain and wine to skilled labour and transport, and prescribing death for anyone who charged more. Issued from the east, probably Antioch, and posted publicly in Greek and Latin across the empire, it responded to decades of currency debasement that had driven prices sharply upward, especially wherever the army had to be supplied.

The edict said nothing about the underlying causes of inflation, and enforcement proved impossible: goods simply vanished from open markets, driven into black-market trade or barter, and surviving evidence suggests it was quietly abandoned within a few years. It remains, nonetheless, one of the most detailed surviving records of prices and wages anywhere in the ancient world.
